title: Final design of the ITER outer vessel steady-state magnetic sensors
closest_feature: Manuscript's general 'Hall sensor deployed for steady-state in-vessel/ex-vessel magnetic field monitoring in a fusion device' concept
delta: Describes the ITER Outer Vessel Steady-state Sensor (OVSS) subsystem: a 60-unit poloidal array welded to the ITER vacuum-vessel outer surface, each containing a pair of BISMUTH Hall sensors (poloidal + normal axes) plus an onboard thermocouple, tested to +-7 T at ITER-relevant temperature/neutron conditions. Bismuth, not GaN/AlGaN; ex-vessel/outer-vessel-surface mounting, not the manuscript's plasma-edge in-vessel placement; uses AC lock-in current-spinning signal processing (an excluded concept per IP_SCOPE.md, noted as third-party context only).

Verified via multiple corroborating abstract sources (ScienceDirect, ResearchGate) since the ScienceDirect abstract page itself was not directly fetchable in this session; content cross-confirmed by the companion calibration paper S020. Confirms a large-scale, mature Hall-sensor magnetic-diagnostic engineering program exists for ITER, using bismuth rather than any III-nitride semiconductor.

title: Graphit[e]-ceramic RF Faraday-thermal shield and plasma limiter
closest_feature: Manuscript's grounded graphite shield installed over the packaged sensor module to reduce arcing and epoxy degradation during GDC/plasma operation (F16) - THE SINGLE MOST ENABLEMENT-THIN AND HIGHEST-PRIORITY ELEMENT PER STAGE 00/10
delta: CLOSEST FUSION-SPECIFIC ANALOG FOUND for a graphite-based shield protecting an in-vessel component from plasma effects. Describes a brazed graphite-to-ceramic (Al2O3 or Macor, via a Ag/Cu/Ti braze alloy) composite functioning as a Faraday-thermal shield and plasma limiter, explicitly identified for use in 'Magnetic Fusion Devices (e.g., Princeton Large Torus Tokamak).' Tested to 40 MW/m^2 thermal flux via electron-gun simulation without joint damage. Assignee: U.S. Department of Energy; inventors D.L.Q. Hwang, J.C. Hosea.
notes: MATERIAL DELTA: this patent's graphite-ceramic composite protects an RF antenna/plasma-limiter structure (an actively plasma-facing component carrying RF/thermal loads) via a brazed, load-bearing thermal-and-electrical shield; the manuscript's element is a GROUNDED graphite shield installed OVER a separately-packaged, epoxy-potted sensor module specifically to prevent GDC/plasma-induced ARCING and EPOXY DEGRADATION of that package - a materially different failure mode (electrical arcing/epoxy chemical degradation of a nearby encapsulated component, not direct plasma-facing thermal/RF shielding of the shield material itself). No brazing, no direct plasma-facing/limiter function, and no epoxy-protection purpose is described in this patent. This is the closest reference found, but the specific combination in F16 (grounded graphite shield + protects an encapsulated epoxy-potted Hall sensor + against GDC arcing/epoxy degradation) was not found anywhere in this search - see search log saturation statement for coverage_area uhv_package.

title: Electron beam gun with grounded shield to prevent arc down
closest_feature: The general electrical-engineering principle underlying the manuscript's grounded-shield-prevents-arcing rationale (F16/F41)
delta: General (non-fusion, non-sensor) vacuum-engineering precedent for the underlying physics: a grounded metal shield placed within one electron mean-free-path of high-voltage surfaces suppresses arc-down/glow-discharge formation by starving the secondary-electron-avalanche ('Geiger discharge') mechanism of amplifiable current. Applied here to an electron-beam gun's filament/emitter structure in a vacuum furnace, not to a sensor package.
notes: GENERAL BACKGROUND ONLY - not fusion-specific and not sensor-specific. Establishes that 'ground a conductive shield near a component to suppress arcing in vacuum/low-pressure discharge conditions' is a well-known, decades-old general engineering principle across vacuum-technology fields, which is directly relevant to Stage 30/40's obviousness analysis of the manuscript's shield (a skilled UHV/plasma engineer would be expected to know this general principle; the open question per IP_SCOPE.md is whether the SPECIFIC application/geometry/placement chosen for this manuscript's shield goes beyond applying this known principle in a predictable way).

closest_feature: THE SINGLE CLOSEST PRE-EXISTING ANALOG FOUND for the manuscript's cover-letter claim (F49): 'the first GaN-based Hall-effect sensor deployed inside a stellarator for in-situ magnetic field monitoring.' This 2014 paper reports a 16-element linear array of miniature GALLIUM ARSENIDE (GaAs, not GaN) Hall sensors mounted on a rotatable PCB inside a re-entrant stainless-steel tube sheathed in boron nitride, INSERTED IN-VESSEL in the Compact Toroidal Hybrid (CTH) device at Auburn University to directly measure the poloidal magnetic field for equilibrium/current-profile reconstruction in a fully three-dimensional plasma.

CTH is explicitly described in this paper as a 'non-axisymmetric hybrid torsatron/tokamak' device, i.e. stellarator-class (3D, non-axisymmetric magnetic field) but not identically labeled 'stellarator' the way HSX is - a precise, material distinction, not a technicality to gloss over. Directly relevant to how narrowly Stage 30 should read F49.
